subtitle: This course examines how connected policies and everyday processes in human services can combine to create racial inequities. From there, you will develop a supported improvement that responds to what you find.
scope: For leaders across DHS who examine policy, service access, resources or workplace practices. This optional course uses sample evidence and decisions to teach structural inquiry. It does not establish a finding about an actual DHS program or person, decide a legal claim, authorize access to records or replace the applicable agency equity-analysis and formal decision processes. Staff own their work with consultant guidance when useful. Individual cultural assessments are not personnel measures. Native American or Tribal-specific matters are excluded and go to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).
introTranscript: An inequitable result can involve more than one interaction. A notice, contact schedule, documentation step, resource decision and wider condition may reinforce one another, even when staff intend to help. Structural racism concerns racial inequity built into connected systems and practices, rather than only individual prejudice. Leaders need to examine those connections without turning a population pattern into a personal judgment or declaring a cause before the evidence supports it. This course follows a practice service process from an observed gap through process mapping, evidence, affected perspectives, alternatives and follow-through. You will practice asking what the agency controls, what requires another responsible route and how a supported improvement can be reviewed honestly. The aim is clear responsibility and meaningful change alongside continued learning.

lessons.title: Look beyond the single interaction
lessons.summary: Distinguish individual conduct, an institutional practice and connected structures while keeping responsibility clear.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an individual action, an institutional practice and a structural connection in a practice case.
objectives: Distinguish an individual action, an institutional practice and a structural connection in a practice case.
Explain why helpful intent does not establish that a process has equitable effects.
Write a structural inquiry question without assigning a motive or cultural stage to a person.
takeaways: Connected rules and resources can matter beyond a single encounter.
Intent and effect are different questions that both deserve accurate attention.
A structural inquiry examines the process and evidence without creating a personal moral or cultural score.
lessons.statement: Ask what connected practices produce the result, not only who meant well or who is easiest to blame.

image.caption: Colleagues examine how a decision connects with the wider process and its evidence.

intro.heading: What lies beyond the encounter?
intro.body:
A practice DSD team receives a concern that some people cannot complete a service renewal. The first discussion focuses on whether one staff member explained the process politely. Respectful communication matters, but the renewal also involves a notice, a deadline, available contact times, a document request and an authorized decision. People encounter those steps under different circumstances. If the team examines only the final conversation, it may miss a recurring barrier created earlier in the process or a connection with wider conditions.

Structural racism concerns how racial inequities can be built into connected policies, practices and systems. The Minnesota Department of Health’s public health-equity explanation distinguishes systems and policy from individual prejudice. Its 2014 report describes historical, cultural, institutional and interpersonal dynamics that can reinforce racial advantage and disadvantage. These sources provide a public Minnesota framework for inquiry. This course does not use their historical figures as current DHS statistics or establish a finding about a particular service from the definition alone.

Keep several levels distinct. An individual action is what a person says or does in an encounter. An institutional practice is a rule, procedure or recurring arrangement within an organization, such as the way contact times are offered. A structural connection involves how institutions, resources and wider conditions interact, such as a contact arrangement combined with work schedules, transportation or other access conditions. These levels can influence one another. They are not excuses for harmful conduct or reasons to treat every difficulty as a single cause.

Helpful intent is important information about what someone hoped to do, but it does not prove the result was equitable. A team may choose one channel to make processing easier and unintentionally make participation harder for some people. Conversely, a racial difference in a summary does not automatically prove what caused it or establish every individual’s motive. Examine the difference, the actual steps, the people’s experience and the responsible requirements. The inquiry should be serious enough to find a barrier and disciplined enough to preserve uncertainty.

Avoid turning the conversation into a test of whether a colleague is a good or bad person. A leader can ask, “Which part of this process creates the difficulty, for whom, and under what conditions?” That question directs attention to something the agency can examine. It does not deny racism or require the leader to infer a person’s inner beliefs. A concern about actual protected-class conduct still proceeds through the responsible formal route. Optional structural learning cannot replace that duty or determine the outcome of a real case.

The racial dimension should not disappear behind a general access discussion. If appropriate evidence shows different results by race, examine that pattern rather than assuming an overall average describes everyone. Ask how a policy or routine may interact with unequal conditions and histories, while preserving the actual data’s limits. Do not treat race as a biological explanation for an outcome or infer a person’s experience from a category. A group-level inquiry and individual listening serve different purposes and can both help a leader reason accurately.

Personal reflection belongs here too. Which part of the process did you initially consider normal or neutral? Whose knowledge made you reconsider it? What did you assume about a person who missed a deadline? Reflecting on those questions can support growth and a better next decision. It is not an IDI assessment or a personnel label. Staff should build their own capacity to examine the process, with consultant guidance and feedback when useful, rather than have every inquiry done for them.

Start with one precise question. The practice team could ask which renewal step people struggle to complete and whether the difficulty differs across relevant experiences in an appropriately authorized review. It should name the decision role and keep current eligibility, records and reporting requirements active. The definition of structural racism helps the team look for connected mechanisms. The actual evidence and responsible process determine what it can support and what should happen next.

inThisLesson: Keep race visible without a personal profile.
lessons.keyStatement: A structural question examines connected mechanisms and racial effects without substituting a personal judgment for evidence.

flashcards.back: A person’s conduct in an encounter; relevant but not the whole process.
A recurring rule, procedure or arrangement within an organization that can shape opportunity and access.
The interaction of policies, institutions, resources and wider conditions that can reinforce an outcome.
A described difference in appropriate evidence that needs examination of scope, quality and possible explanations.
A conclusion whose strength and scope match the actual evidence and responsible analysis.

accordion.heading: Keep the levels connected and distinct

items.title: One encounter matters
items.body: A staff member explains a step inaccurately. The explanation deserves attention, and a formal concern must retain its appropriate route. The leader should also ask whether the notice, training or contact arrangement made the same problem likely in other encounters. Correcting one explanation can be useful while leaving a recurring process unchanged. A structural inquiry adds those questions; it does not erase individual responsibility or assume that every staff member behaved in the same way.

items.title: A recurring practice matters
items.body: The program offers a single contact channel because it is familiar to the team. Ask how the channel works for the task and what actual feedback or authorized evidence shows. A common arrangement is not automatically an equitable one, but inconvenience alone does not establish every racial mechanism. Identify the relevant process, possible differences in effect and the requirement or authority behind the arrangement before developing alternatives.

items.title: Connected conditions matter
items.body: A document request, contact schedule and wider access conditions can reinforce difficulty. The team may control one step and need another responsible role for a different step. Map the relationship rather than claim that the agency controls every condition or that a wider issue makes agency action impossible. A bounded improvement can matter when it targets an actual mechanism and preserves the questions that remain outside the immediate decision.

tabs.label: Only intent is examined
tabs.body: The leader concludes the process is equitable because staff are trying to help. This values goodwill but leaves effects and recurring mechanisms unexamined. Ask what happens at the actual steps, which experience is missing and whether an authorized review shows a racial pattern. A serious inquiry can respect colleagues’ intent while identifying a process that needs change. It does not require a personal accusation to begin examining the result.

tabs.label: A cause is declared immediately
tabs.body: The leader sees a difference and announces that one employee caused structural racism. The concern may warrant attention, but the conclusion leaps across levels and assigns a cause without examining evidence. Separate the individual conduct, institutional arrangement and wider connection. Use the actual formal route for a protected-class concern and the responsible analysis process for the policy question, without making either inquiry wait for a course exercise.

tabs.label: Mechanisms and evidence guide inquiry
tabs.body: The leader names an observed concern, maps possible connected steps and asks what evidence would distinguish explanations. The inquiry keeps the racial dimension visible while avoiding a personal cultural label or universal claim. It can lead to a bounded improvement, a formal referral or a request for further evidence. The strength comes from clear reasoning and responsibility, not certainty produced before the work has been examined.

check.question: A team’s intent is to help, but a service process may have unequal racial effects. What should a leader do?
check.correct: Examine the actual steps, appropriate evidence and affected experience, keeping intent, effects and formal responsibilities distinct.
wrong: Treat helpful intent as proof that every effect is equitable.
Infer each colleague’s motive and IDI orientation from the summary.
Ignore racial patterns because only individual interactions can matter.
check.feedbackCorrect: This makes a serious structural inquiry possible without replacing evidence with a personal judgment.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Good intent does not establish the effect. A summary is not evidence of each person’s motives or an IDI assessment. Ignoring a racial pattern can leave connected practices unexamined. Ask which mechanisms and evidence matter, preserve actual formal duties and match any conclusion to the support the inquiry provides.

items.text: A staff member gives an inaccurate explanation in one encounter.
The program repeatedly offers only one contact channel.
A contact arrangement interacts with wider transportation and work-schedule conditions.
A colleague asks a neutral clarification instead of assigning a personal motive.
The notice uses a recurring document sequence set by the program.
Resource decisions and several institutions’ access arrangements reinforce difficulty.

lessons.next: Next, map how a service process can accumulate burden across several steps.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Devon receives a renewal-access concern. The team says its staff are polite, so the process cannot have an inequitable effect. Devon knows the process also includes notice wording, contact times and document requests. No current evidence yet establishes the cause or every person’s experience, and any formal protected-class concern has its own route.
scenario.prompt: Which first response would support a credible inquiry?
options: Map the relevant steps and evidence, examine affected experience and keep formal duties active without assigning personal cultural labels.
End the inquiry because good intentions guarantee an equitable process.
Declare every staff member at Denial and treat the label as the finding.
responses: This keeps the question serious, specific and examinable while preserving responsibility and uncertainty.
The response substitutes intent for effects and leaves the actual concern unexamined.
The summary is not a personal assessment. A cultural label does not identify the mechanism or satisfy formal duties.

lessons.transfer: Choose one practice or authorized process concern. Write an individual action, an institutional practice and a wider connection that the inquiry should distinguish.

move.control: You can ask a precise process question and examine the evidence without reducing the issue to intent or a personal label.
move.failure: Goodwill is treated as proof, or an unsupported personal judgment takes the place of a structural inquiry.
move.next: Frame one question about connected practices, racial effects and the evidence needed to support a responsible conclusion.

lessons.title: Map the process and its accumulated burden
lessons.summary: Trace a service journey, identify connected conditions and locate the agency choices that can be examined.
lessons.objective: Map at least four connected steps in a practice human-services process.
objectives: Map at least four connected steps in a practice human-services process.
Identify how separately manageable steps can accumulate difficulty under different conditions.
Distinguish a change within a team’s authority from a concern requiring another responsible role.
takeaways: A barrier may emerge from the sequence rather than a single step alone.
Historical and wider conditions can shape how the same process is encountered.
An accurate map names actual requirements, choices and decision authority.
lessons.statement: Trace what a person must do and which decisions created the sequence before deciding where to act.

image.caption: A process map connects the task, its requirements and the choices the responsible team can examine.

intro.heading: How do the steps work together?
intro.body:
A practice DSD renewal process sends a notice, asks the person to call during a limited contact period, requires a document and records a decision. Each step has a stated purpose. The notice communicates the renewal, the call clarifies a question, the document provides needed evidence and the decision follows the responsible process. Yet the sequence may create a burden that the team cannot see by reviewing each step separately. If the notice is hard to understand, the person may use the contact period to discover the document requirement too late to complete it.

Map the actual journey in plain language. What does the person receive, understand, do, wait for and receive next? Which step requires another institution or resource? Where can the person ask a question? What happens when a step cannot be completed as expected? The course’s example is practice and does not state a real DHS renewal rule. In actual work, confirm the current applicable requirements and use an authorized review process rather than rely on a remembered sequence or change a deadline informally.

Distinguish a requirement from an agency choice and a local habit. The underlying rule may require certain evidence. The notice’s order may be a design choice. A staff member’s familiar shorthand may be a local habit rather than required wording. A clear map prevents a habit from being defended as law and a legal requirement from being changed as if it were merely a preference. If the source or authority is uncertain, record the question and ask the responsible role rather than fill the gap with a confident assumption.

Examine accumulated burden. A person may need to understand a notice, reach a contact, obtain a document elsewhere and return it through an available channel. Time, access, resources and another institution’s arrangement may interact. The point is not to assume that a racial category tells you the person’s circumstances. It is to examine how a process may interact with unequal conditions and whether appropriate evidence shows a racial pattern. An average completion rate can miss the step where difficulty is concentrated.

Historical policy can also provide context for why conditions are unequal. The Federal Reserve’s historical account describes public and private redlining and the role of federal housing policy in restricting credit in Black-populated neighborhoods. This is a documented historical example of connected institutional rules shaping access, not evidence that a particular practice renewal result was caused by that history. Use historical context to widen the inquiry and identify a possible relationship. The current process still needs its own evidence, source quality and responsible analysis.

Do not make the map a story of individual failure. “People did not respond” describes a result but does not explain why. The notice may not have reached the intended audience, the next action may be unclear, the channel may be difficult to use or the person may have a different reason. Ask what evidence could distinguish these possibilities. Missing information is a limit, not permission to invent a cultural explanation, label a community uninterested or assume every nonresponse has the same cause.

Locate the agency choices. The team may be able to clarify a sequence through the approved notice process, while a policy office holds authority over an evidence requirement. A broader resource issue may need leadership or another institution. Identify the responsible role and a useful next question at each point. A structural issue does not mean every improvement must be total before any action is worthwhile. It means the leader should understand how a bounded change connects to the wider process and what it cannot solve by itself.

Use a proportionate map that can guide action. Start with one service journey and the decision under review. Preserve required content, privacy and formal procedures. Include the experience of people who struggled or never reached the service through appropriate arrangements, without requesting unnecessary personal histories. Staff can do the mapping and seek consultant feedback on the reasoning. The result should make choices and connections clearer, not become an elaborate diagram that conceals the next responsible step.

inThisLesson: Distinguish a rule, design choice and habit.
Examine accumulated burden and historical context.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful map shows both the connected burden and the specific authority for each possible change.

items.title: A step with a legitimate purpose
items.body: A document request can have a real evidence purpose. The structural inquiry does not assume every requirement should disappear. Ask whether the current sequence and explanation support the purpose, whether another authorized option addresses a barrier and who can consider it. Preserve accuracy and the actual rule. A clear distinction between requirement and design choice helps avoid both dismissing a concern and promising a change the team cannot make.

items.title: A connection the average hides
items.body: A notice, contact schedule and outside document source may each appear manageable in isolation. Together they can create delay or a missed step. Examine where the journey changes, using appropriate evidence and relevant feedback rather than a cultural guess. If a racial pattern is present, ask which mechanisms could account for it and what information would help distinguish them. A map makes a possible connection visible but does not prove a cause by itself.

items.title: A concern outside the immediate scope
items.body: The team may identify a wider resource condition it cannot change alone. Record the concern with its evidence and identify the responsible role or route. Do not use the wider condition to claim the agency’s own notice or channel choices are irrelevant. A bounded change can reduce one burden while another question remains. Explain both so the review does not present a limited revision as a complete structural remedy or pretend no useful action is possible.

tabs.label: Every step is reviewed alone
tabs.body: The team checks that each step has a purpose and concludes the process is sound. This can miss how order, waiting and another institution’s arrangements interact. Map the whole journey and examine where people actually encounter difficulty. A legitimate purpose does not establish that the sequence is the only authorized way to achieve it or that its effects are the same under different conditions.

tabs.label: All requirements are removed informally
tabs.body: The team sees a burden and tells staff to disregard the rule, evidence or formal decision process. The concern deserves attention, but a course does not authorize an exception or a policy change. Identify the source and responsible role, compare available options and route any proposed requirement change appropriately. An improvement should address the mechanism while preserving actual authority, accuracy and accountability.

tabs.label: The journey and authority are connected
tabs.body: The team maps the person’s tasks, the relevant institutional connections, current requirements and choices within authority. It then selects an evidence question and a responsible next action. This approach can reveal a cumulative burden without declaring every step invalid or every outcome explained. It supports a bounded improvement and a wider referral when needed, with honest limits rather than a universal remedy claim.

check.question: Several service steps may create a cumulative burden. What makes the map useful?
check.correct: Trace the connected tasks and conditions, distinguish requirements from choices and identify the responsible role for each proposed change.
wrong: Treat every familiar practice as a legal requirement without checking a source.
Remove actual requirements informally because any burden proves they are invalid.
Review each step alone and assume their interaction cannot matter.
check.feedbackCorrect: This connects the journey with actual authority and creates a practical basis for evidence and alternatives.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A familiar habit is not automatically law. A burden does not authorize staff to disregard a requirement. Reviewing steps separately can hide the effect of their order and connections. Confirm the actual source, examine the person’s journey and identify which responsible process can consider a supported change.

sorting.heading: Locate the type of process feature

items.text: The rule specifies evidence needed for the formal decision.
The team chooses where a notice explains the next contact.
The contact schedule interacts with another institution’s document availability.
A current source sets the formal decision procedure.
The agency selects an available communication channel through its process.
A sequence interacts with wider resource and transportation conditions.

lessons.next: Next, examine what the available figures can support and what the inquiry still needs to learn.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Alina maps a renewal notice, a contact period, an outside document request and a decision. The team controls notice order through its approved process but not the underlying evidence rule. A colleague wants to change the rule informally, while another says every step has a purpose so there cannot be a barrier.
options: Stop the inquiry because each step has a purpose.
Tell staff to ignore the evidence rule without the responsible process.
Examine the connected burden and source requirements, identify the authorized notice choice and route any proposed rule change to its responsible role.
responses: A purpose for each step does not explain the effect of the sequence or its interaction with wider conditions.
The course does not authorize a formal rule exception. The concern needs a responsible analysis and decision route.
This makes the actual choices and limits visible and gives the team a supported way to continue the inquiry.

lessons.transfer: Map one practice or authorized journey in five steps. At each step, identify a requirement, a choice or a connection that needs confirmation.

move.control: You can clarify the journey, evidence question and decision authority without removing rules or treating habits as law.
move.failure: The team misses a connected burden or promises a change beyond its authority.
move.next: Confirm one requirement’s source and one design choice’s responsible role before proposing a bounded improvement.

lessons.title: Read a racial pattern without overstating its cause
lessons.summary: Examine denominators, process stages, missing information and the difference between a pattern and a supported explanation.
lessons.objective: Calculate and distinguish two practice completion rates and their percentage-point difference.
objectives: Calculate and distinguish two practice completion rates and their percentage-point difference.
Identify two reasons a summary may be insufficient to explain a racial pattern.
State an evidence question and privacy boundary for an authorized further inquiry.
takeaways: Counts need a relevant denominator and comparable scope.
An observed racial difference deserves examination without automatically proving its cause.
Missing information remains unknown, and actual data use requires authority and safeguards.
lessons.statement: A credible analysis makes the pattern clear and keeps the unanswered question equally clear.

image.caption: A careful review connects figures with their definitions, scope and remaining questions.

intro.heading: What can these numbers actually establish?
intro.body:
A practice training dataset shows that 80 of 100 people in one group completed a step and 60 of 100 in another group completed the same step during a defined practice period. The completion rates are 80 percent and 60 percent. The difference is 20 percentage points, calculated by subtracting the two rates. These invented figures support a practice description of a gap. They do not describe an actual DHS racial outcome, establish what caused a difference or predict any individual’s result.

The denominator matters. Eighty completions out of 100 people offered the step means something different from 80 completions out of 200. Confirm who was included, which period is covered and what completion means. If one group is measured after the first notice and another after a later assistance step, the rates are not a simple like-for-like comparison. A clear definition can prevent an attractive chart from overstating what the evidence actually measures.

Race may be relevant to an authorized equity inquiry, but it should not be inferred from names, accents or a leader’s impressions. Use appropriate approved information and responsible data practices for an actual analysis. Categories, missing values and reporting choices need examination. Combining distinct experiences into one broad group may hide a pattern, while presenting very small or identifiable information may create a privacy problem. This course does not set a numerical disclosure threshold or authorize collection of new personal information.

Locate the process stage. An overall completion difference may reflect who received the notice, who understood it, who reached assistance, who could obtain the document or how a decision was recorded. An aggregate count cannot show every mechanism. The inquiry may need a proportionate authorized view of stages and relevant experience to distinguish possible explanations. Do not assume that the last staff interaction caused the whole gap or that a wider condition makes agency choices irrelevant.

Keep the possible explanations visible. A delivery problem, an unclear instruction, an inaccessible channel, different process timing and other conditions could affect the result. Some explanations may interact with historically unequal resources and produce a racial pattern. A serious analysis asks what evidence supports a proposed connection and what would challenge it. A disparity is a signal to investigate, not a completed causal finding. The distinction does not minimize the concern; it helps make the recommended action credible.

Missing information should not become reassurance or blame. If the team has no account from people who did not complete the step, it cannot say they approved the process or lacked interest. If one category has incomplete data, explain that limit. If a change in data collection makes periods differ, do not treat the apparent trend as a verified improvement without checking comparability. A report should name the gap in evidence and a responsible way to examine it rather than fill it with a cultural story.

Use a working statement with three parts: the observation, the limit and the next question. For the sample figures, the statement could say that the defined completion rates differ by 20 percentage points, that the figures do not explain the cause and that the next inquiry concerns where the process diverges and what participants experienced. For real work, the responsible data and analysis process determines what can be accessed and reported. The learning method is not a permission slip to inspect identifiable records.

Leaders can make the reasoning accessible without making it simplistic. Explain percentages in relation to the people or events measured, distinguish a percentage-point difference from a relative change and state uncertainty plainly. Do not use a population result as an IDI diagnosis, performance label or assessment of a community’s values. Staff should be able to conduct a proportionate inquiry, ask for responsible technical support and seek consultant feedback while retaining the work. Good evidence supports a better question and a better next action, not an unsupported certainty claim.

inThisLesson: Distinguish a pattern from its cause.
Preserve missing information and data authority.
lessons.keyStatement: Describe the observed pattern, its limits and the evidence question before declaring an explanation.

items.title: A count needs a denominator
items.body: A report lists 80 completions in one group and 60 in another. Before comparing results, ask how many people or events were eligible for the measure and whether the definitions match. Equal denominators in the practice exercise make the practice rate calculation straightforward; actual data may not. A clear denominator prevents volume from being mistaken for opportunity or success and helps the reader understand what the figure does and does not measure.

items.title: A racial pattern needs a mechanism inquiry
items.body: An appropriately authorized summary may show different results by race. That difference deserves attention, but the table alone does not establish the process mechanism or every individual’s experience. Compare relevant stages, requirements and actual feedback through responsible methods. Ask what evidence would support or challenge each explanation. Naming uncertainty keeps the analysis credible while preserving a serious question about racial equity rather than dismissing it.

items.title: A missing value needs an honest limit
items.body: A record may have an unknown category, an incomplete process stage or no participant response. Say what is missing and how it affects interpretation. Do not infer identity or approval to make the chart complete. A leader can identify an authorized next inquiry or seek responsible data guidance. The course creates no collection permission, disclosure threshold or requirement to share personal information in a learning exercise.

tabs.label: The table proves a cause
tabs.body: The leader declares that the practice difference proves one staff member’s intent or one community’s lack of interest. The numbers describe completion under the exercise definitions; they do not supply either explanation. Examine the stage, connected conditions and actual experience. A supported finding needs more than a striking gap, and a formal concern must retain its responsible process rather than be settled through a practice calculation.

tabs.label: The gap is dismissed as ordinary variation
tabs.body: The leader says averages always differ and therefore no inquiry is needed. Uncertainty about cause is real, but it does not make an observed racial pattern irrelevant. Check data quality, definitions and scope, then ask which evidence would help examine a possible barrier. A proportionate investigation can respect uncertainty and still take the equity question seriously without promising a causal conclusion in advance.

tabs.label: Observation and inquiry are separated
tabs.body: The leader describes the practice rates, their 20-percentage-point difference, the defined scope and the unanswered cause question. The next step examines relevant stages and experience through the responsible data process. This account makes the concern visible while protecting privacy and inference limits. The reasoning can then support a bounded option or a request for further evidence without a personal cultural label or universal success claim.

check.question: In the practice example, 80 of 100 people in one group and 60 of 100 in another complete the same defined step. What is supported?
check.correct: The rates are 80 percent and 60 percent, a 20-percentage-point difference; the figures do not establish the cause.
wrong: The difference is 20 completed people regardless of any denominator, so the denominator never matters.
The figures prove every person in the lower-rate group lacks interest.
The gap proves a particular employee’s motive and assessed IDI position.
check.feedbackCorrect: The calculation uses the exercise’s comparable denominators and states the pattern without inventing an explanation.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The exercise’s counts happen to differ by 20, but a rate still depends on its denominator and definition. Group results do not reveal each person’s interest. A summary cannot establish an employee’s motive or cultural assessment. State the observation, check comparability and identify the evidence needed to examine possible process mechanisms.

items.text: In the defined exercise, the rates differ by 20 percentage points.
At which process stage does the difference emerge?
Every nonresponse proves agreement with the notice.
The exercise counts are 80 of 100 and 60 of 100.
Do the periods, definitions and available information support comparison?
A racial category determines an individual’s motivation.

lessons.next: Next, combine relevant lived experience, source context and decision authority without treating one voice as universal.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Simone reviews the invented 80-of-100 and 60-of-100 completion exercise. The scope and step definitions match, but the exercise does not explain the cause. A colleague wants to label the lower-rate group uninterested; another wants to declare all staff at one IDI stage. Real data access is not part of the exercise.
scenario.prompt: Which response uses the figures accurately?
options: Describe the 20-percentage-point gap, preserve the unknown cause and identify a responsible inquiry into process stages and experience.
Assign an interest level to every individual from the group rate.
Treat the gap as an assessed IDI result for the workforce.
responses: This makes the pattern and limits clear and turns the calculation into a useful next question.
The rate is not evidence of every person’s motivation and does not establish why the step was incomplete.
The exercise is not a cultural assessment. Personnel labels cannot replace analysis of the actual mechanism.

lessons.transfer: Write an observation, a limit and a next evidence question for one practice or authorized measure. Which denominator and definition does the reader need?

move.control: You can make a figure understandable and identify an authorized next inquiry without inferring identity, motive or cause.
move.failure: A count is mistaken for a comparable rate, missing information becomes reassurance or a pattern becomes a personal judgment.
move.next: Check one measure’s denominator, period, definition and source before using it to support an option or conclusion.

lessons.title: Bring affected knowledge into the decision
lessons.summary: Connect lived experience and other evidence with an honest participation role and a visible agency response.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an individual’s account, an organization’s perspective and process evidence in a practice inquiry.
objectives: Distinguish an individual’s account, an organization’s perspective and process evidence in a practice inquiry.
Write an invitation that states the choice participants can influence and the responsible decision role.
Identify a missing perspective without requiring a personal disclosure or claiming universal representation.
takeaways: Affected knowledge can identify a mechanism a summary misses.
One voice is useful within its scope and does not represent everyone.
Participation matters when the agency can explain the open choice and response.
lessons.statement: Invite knowledge about a real choice, then show how the responsible decision used it.

image.caption: A participation plan can examine whose relevant experience remains unheard.

intro.heading: What knowledge can change the decision?
intro.body:
A practice DSD team sees a completion difference and asks a familiar partner to review the process. The partner identifies an instruction that may be confusing. An individual describes difficulty reaching the contact route. Another person says the instruction was clear but the required document took longer to obtain. These accounts do not have to agree to be useful. They may identify different mechanisms or conditions. The leader’s task is to preserve their scope, connect them with other evidence and explain what the team can actually change.

Affected experience is more than an illustrative story for a finished recommendation. It can help define the question, locate a process step, compare options and understand whether a change was useful. Invite people while a meaningful choice remains open. If the underlying rule is outside the team’s authority, say so and name the route for that concern. Do not ask participants to redesign eligibility when the available decision concerns the notice’s sequence or contact explanation.

Different sources contribute different kinds of knowledge. An individual may describe what happened in one service journey. An organization may identify patterns from its work or concerns within its mission. Administrative evidence may describe a defined step across a period. A policy source states requirements. None automatically cancels the others or answers every question. Examine where the accounts align, differ or leave something unknown, using an authorized process and proportionate privacy protections.

Do not decide that a voice is authentic only when it confirms the leader’s expectation about race or culture. A person may describe a successful experience, a barrier, a different priority or a concern about the proposed option. The analysis should examine the work reasons rather than rank people by how well they fit a presumed community story. A racial equity inquiry can keep race and systemic patterns visible while respecting varied individual experiences and avoiding a personal cultural profile.

The invitation should state what can change, who decides and what response participants can expect through the actual arrangement. “Tell us whether the next-step wording is understandable before the notice is finalized” offers a clearer role than “help transform the entire system” when only a sentence can be revised. If the decision is already final, provide accurate information and a route for concerns rather than calling the announcement shared design. An honest limit supports participation better than an expansive promise the agency cannot keep.

Examine missing experience. The usual participants may be people who reached the service, have an established relationship with the agency or could attend at the chosen time. People who did not complete an earlier step may know about a different barrier. Ask how to hear relevant experience through appropriate arrangements. Do not require people to disclose immigration status, medical information or a workplace concern in an open learning group to make their contribution count. Formal needs and concerns retain their separate responsible processes.

Participation also requires a response. The team can explain which suggestion changed the notice, which concern requires another office and why an option was not selected. Agreement is not guaranteed, but a visible account can keep input from disappearing between roles. Do not claim every community agreed with the decision because one organization helped recruit participants. Describe the actual contribution, the reasoning and the gap that remains. A clear response is part of accountable agency work, not a cultural assessment of participants.

Staff should perform this inquiry as part of building their own capacity. The consultant can help sharpen the question, examine evidence and provide feedback. A leader can arrange the decision role, time and appropriate support without transferring every staff task to the consultant or requiring a universal consultant review gate. The result should connect knowledge with action: a revised option, an evidence question, a formal referral or an explained limit that the agency can stand behind.

lessons.keyStatement: A contribution has a meaningful role when the choice, authority and response are clear.

accordion.heading: Keep the knowledge and response connected

items.title: An account can identify a mechanism
items.body: A person explains that the next-step instruction was understandable but the contact route did not work during the available period. This can direct attention to a different step from the one the team first suspected. Preserve the account’s actual scope and compare it with other evidence. Do not turn one account into everyone’s experience or dismiss it because it differs from the leader’s preferred explanation of the racial pattern.

items.title: An organization has a scope
items.body: A trusted partner may see recurring navigation concerns and may help improve the inquiry. Its mission and knowledge can be valuable without giving it authority to approve every agency decision or speak for every affected individual. State the contribution actually agreed to, identify missing experience and make the response visible. A bounded partnership is more credible than a universal representation claim added to make the report look complete.

items.title: A limit can still receive a response
items.body: Participants may identify a concern with a requirement outside the team’s immediate authority. Record the relevant concern and route it appropriately instead of promising an informal exception or pretending the concern does not matter. Explain what the present review can change and what remains with another role. An honest response can recognize the issue, preserve the actual rule and keep a useful next inquiry visible.

tabs.label: The recommendation is already fixed
tabs.body: The team asks participants for advice after deciding every option and uses their accounts only to decorate the report. People may contribute significant time without a real choice to influence. Clarify whether the activity is information, advice or shared development, and keep an actual decision open when seeking influence. The analysis should explain what input changed and what remains constrained rather than present attendance as approval.

tabs.label: One account becomes the whole explanation
tabs.body: The team receives a compelling story and treats it as the cause of every racial difference. The account may reveal an important mechanism but still needs its scope and comparison with other evidence. Ask where the experience fits in the process and which other conditions are relevant. Preserving a story’s limits protects both the person’s contribution and the credibility of the recommendation.

tabs.label: Knowledge informs an open choice
tabs.body: The team states an available notice or process choice, invites relevant perspectives through appropriate arrangements and connects their accounts with requirements and other evidence. The authorized decision role then explains the option selected, concerns routed elsewhere and the review question. This design supports meaningful participation without promising unanimity, demanding personal disclosures or turning cultural identity into a legitimacy test.

check.question: How should a leader use differing participant accounts in a structural inquiry?
check.correct: Preserve each account’s scope, examine the mechanisms and other evidence, and explain the responsible decision and response.
wrong: Choose only the account that matches a presumed racial or cultural story.
Claim one partner’s advice proves universal community agreement.
Require sensitive personal histories in an open group before input can count.
check.feedbackCorrect: The approach keeps varied knowledge useful and connects it with an actual decision rather than an expected identity performance.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A presumed group story is not a sound test of evidence. A partner’s advice does not establish universal approval. Sensitive personal disclosure should not be imposed to legitimize input in a learning group. Ask about the actual task, preserve privacy and source scope, and state how the authorized process considered the contribution.

sorting.heading: Locate the contribution or next question

items.text: A person describes where one service journey became difficult.
The responsible role explains which notice option was selected and why.
One organization’s advice means every community agreed with the result.
A partner identifies a recurring concern within its stated work.
The team routes a proposed eligibility change to its authorized process.
A voice counts only if it matches the leader’s expected cultural account.

lessons.next: Next, compare options against the barrier, evidence, requirements and authority rather than choose a symbolic response alone.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Jonah receives three different accounts about a renewal process. One concerns wording, another the contact route and a third an outside document delay. A partner helped invite participants but did not approve the decision. The team can revise a notice choice through its process; the evidence rule belongs with another responsible role.
options: Select the story that sounds most like the expected community experience and ignore the others.
Compare the accounts with the process and other evidence, keep an actual choice open and explain the authorized response and wider referral.
Claim the partner approved every detail and require participants to share personal histories to be counted.
responses: This uses a stereotype as the evidence test and may erase a relevant mechanism.
This preserves distinct knowledge, connects it with a real decision and keeps limits and responsibility visible.
The claim exceeds the partner’s role, while the disclosure condition adds an unnecessary barrier.

lessons.transfer: Write an invitation for one practice or authorized process choice. State what can change, who decides and how people will hear the response.

move.control: You can create an honest opportunity and examine varied knowledge without a universal representation claim or identity test.
move.failure: Input decorates a settled decision, a single voice becomes universal evidence or participation requires unnecessary personal disclosure.
move.next: Confirm one open choice and responsible response before asking people for their experience or recommendations.

lessons.title: Compare options that address the mechanism
lessons.summary: Develop a practical alternative, preserve requirements and explain tradeoffs, authority and evidence.
lessons.objective: Connect a proposed option to a specific supported or suspected process mechanism.
objectives: Connect a proposed option to a specific supported or suspected process mechanism.
Compare two practice alternatives against effects, constraints and evidence needs.
Identify which formal review or decision role a proposed change requires.
takeaways: An option should address a mechanism rather than only signal concern.
A structural inquiry can support bounded action while a wider question remains.
Actual rules, legal requirements and decision authority remain active.
lessons.statement: Choose an option for the barrier it can address and the evidence that supports it, with an honest account of its limits.

image.caption: An options discussion connects the proposed change with evidence and responsible authority.

intro.heading: What would this option actually change?
intro.body:
A practice DSD team has evidence that a notice sequence is confusing for some readers and a separate question about contact availability. The team proposes adding an equity statement to the notice. The statement may communicate purpose, but it does not automatically clarify the sequence or make the contact route usable. A more useful comparison asks which option changes the suspected mechanism, what evidence supports it, which requirements apply and who can authorize the decision.

Name the mechanism in plain language. “The notice explains the next step after the point where the person needs it” is more useful than “the system is broken.” The broad concern may be serious, but the specific statement lets the team develop and examine an option. “The contact arrangement may interact with people’s available time” is a hypothesis that needs evidence. Do not convert it into a universal cultural explanation or declare the same cause for every racial outcome.

Develop more than one practical alternative. The team might clarify the notice order through its approved process, revise the contact explanation or ask the responsible service role to examine another available arrangement. Compare what each option addresses, what it leaves unchanged and what evidence the next review needs. An option can reduce a burden without solving every structural condition. The report should neither dismiss a bounded improvement as worthless nor present it as a complete remedy for racial inequity.

Keep requirements and authority visible. The underlying evidence rule, statutory deadline or formal decision procedure cannot be disregarded because a course identifies a concern. Determine the actual source and responsible process. A long-term policy or program change may require the applicable DHS equity analysis and leadership decision route. The course’s planning routine is preparation, not a replacement for that requirement or a new customized tool approval. Ask the appropriate role when the scope or procedure is uncertain.

Examine who benefits, who may face a new burden and whose perspective is missing. A clearer digital notice may help some readers while leaving people who do not use the channel unheard. A changed contact arrangement may address one task and affect staff capacity or another service step. These are questions to examine, not reasons to stop. Identify the relevant tradeoff and source of evidence. Do not assume that the option is equitable because its title includes equity or that every person in a racial category will have the same result.

Avoid inventing race-based eligibility, selection or employment rules in a learning exercise. A structural inquiry can examine a racial pattern and develop a barrier-focused alternative while preserving the applicable law and authorized agency process. A proposed remedy that changes rights, criteria or access rules needs responsible legal and policy consideration. The course does not declare a real legal outcome or approve a preferential rule. Serious racial-equity work and accurate authority belong together rather than being framed as opposing goals.

Plan the evidence before claiming success. What would indicate that the selected option was used and helped the task? What might show that it failed or introduced another barrier? Which information can be gathered appropriately, and which uncertainty will remain? A small authorized review can guide a next step without becoming a personnel measure or cultural assessment. Keep sources and participant accounts attached to their scope, and avoid making missing information look favorable just because the team wants the option to succeed.

The leader’s role is to connect reasoning with action. Staff can compare options and own the analysis with consultant feedback. The authorized role considers the actual change, and formal concerns continue through their routes. A clear recommendation can say which option is supported, why, what conditions or review are needed and which wider issue requires another decision. That is more operationally useful than a symbolic statement alone or a promise to transform every system without a responsible plan.

inThisLesson: Name the mechanism an option addresses.
Plan evidence of use and effect.
lessons.keyStatement: A recommendation connects an actual mechanism with an authorized option, evidence and review.

items.title: An option that changes a task
items.body: Reordering a confusing instruction can address a notice mechanism when the responsible process permits the change. Explain what moves, why and which required content remains accurate. Do not claim that a wording change resolves every racial inequity or ignore a separate contact issue. A bounded option is meaningful when its purpose and evidence are clear, and its limitation can point toward another responsible inquiry rather than disappear from the account.

items.title: An option that needs another role
items.body: The team may identify a contact or resource arrangement outside its own authority. Prepare the evidence question and proposed alternative for the responsible service or policy role. A referral should include enough reasoning to be useful without unnecessary personal details. It is not a way to abandon the concern or transfer every staff task to the consultant. The agency can preserve responsibility across roles by naming the next decision and response.

items.title: A tradeoff that needs evidence
items.body: A change can improve one task while affecting another process or available capacity. Identify the possible effect and what approved evidence would help examine it. Do not assume the tradeoff is inevitable, and do not make a reassuring claim before the review. Comparing options should preserve actual requirements, participants’ relevant experience and the decision role. The aim is a supported choice with honest limits, not an option that merely sounds equitable.

tabs.label: A statement without a mechanism change
tabs.body: The team adds an equity message and treats it as the remedy for a confusing sequence. The message may express a legitimate purpose, but it does not show that the next step is clearer or the contact route works. Match the option to the barrier and plan evidence of its use. A symbolic expression can sit alongside practical action, but it should not substitute for the agency decision and review that the concern requires.

tabs.label: An informal exception to every rule
tabs.body: The team responds to the concern by telling staff to ignore deadlines, evidence and authorized decision procedures. This goes beyond optional learning and may create inaccurate or inconsistent outcomes. Confirm the actual source and route a proposed policy change appropriately. A serious structural inquiry can challenge a requirement’s effects without pretending the team has authority to replace it or that the course has approved a new legal rule.

tabs.label: A supported bounded alternative
tabs.body: The team selects an authorized notice revision tied to the identified sequence problem, identifies a separate contact inquiry and plans a proportionate review. It states who decides, which requirements remain and what evidence might challenge the option. This approach keeps racial-equity reasoning connected with practical responsibility. The recommendation can be useful even when a wider condition remains unresolved, because it makes both the immediate action and the next question visible.

check.question: A notice sequence is confusing and contact access remains an open question. What is a supported recommendation?
check.correct: Propose an authorized sequence revision tied to evidence, preserve required content and identify the responsible contact inquiry and review limits.
wrong: Add an equity slogan and declare every mechanism corrected.
Authorize staff to ignore the actual evidence rule without its formal process.
Create a new race-based eligibility rule from the course exercise.
check.feedbackCorrect: The option addresses the identified task, keeps authority accurate and preserves the unresolved mechanism and evidence question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A slogan does not establish that a process changed. An optional course cannot authorize ignoring a rule. It also does not approve a race-based eligibility or employment remedy. Identify the actual mechanism, compare available alternatives and use the responsible policy, legal and decision routes for any change affecting formal criteria or duties.

items.text: Clarify the notice sequence through its approved process.
Confirm which policy role can consider an evidence-rule change.
The new slogan proves every racial inequity is eliminated.
Examine an available contact alternative with relevant evidence.
Complete the applicable formal equity analysis for a qualifying long-term action.
The course authorizes a new eligibility rule without agency or legal review.

lessons.next: Finally, make follow-through clear enough that the next review can distinguish activity, effect and uncertainty.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Keisha has a supported notice-sequence concern and an unresolved contact issue. Her team can revise the notice through its approved process. A colleague suggests only an equity slogan; another suggests ignoring an evidence rule. The proposed long-term action must use its applicable formal agency analysis and decision route.
options: Ignore the evidence rule informally and call the exception the new agency policy.
Use only a slogan so no practical process decision needs attention.
Connect an authorized notice option with evidence, preserve requirements, route the contact question and plan a proportionate review.
responses: The concern does not give the team authority to replace the actual rule or bypass its decision process.
A purpose statement alone does not address the identified sequence or unresolved contact mechanism.
This turns the inquiry into usable action while keeping wider questions, formal requirements and review limits visible.

lessons.transfer: Compare two options for one practice or authorized barrier. State the mechanism, likely effect, constraint, responsible role and evidence needed for each.

move.control: You can connect an option to a specific barrier and preserve the formal decisions it does not authorize.
move.failure: A symbolic statement replaces action, a bounded change is called a universal remedy or the course is used to invent an exception.
move.next: Write a recommendation that names the supported option, actual decision route, unresolved concern and review question.

lessons.title: Review change with accountability and honest limits
lessons.summary: Separate activity, use, effect and uncertainty while assigning a responsible next action.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an activity measure from evidence of process use and effect.
objectives: Distinguish an activity measure from evidence of process use and effect.
Write a bounded review conclusion that preserves missing information and alternative explanations.
Assign an authorized next action while keeping staff ownership and formal duties active.
takeaways: A completed activity is not proof that the mechanism or racial gap changed.
A useful result can be recognized while its scope and uncertainty remain visible.
Follow-through needs a responsible role and another decision, not a personal cultural score.
lessons.statement: Describe what changed, what the evidence supports and who will act on the remaining question.

image.caption: A review can make progress and uncertainty visible in the same account.

intro.heading: What will the next decision use?
intro.body:
A practice DSD team revises a notice, trains staff on the new sequence and asks several readers whether the next step is clearer. The leader has counts of staff receiving the explanation and positive comments from some readers. The leader wants to declare the racial completion gap eliminated and every colleague at Adaptation. The work may represent useful progress, but neither the activity count nor the comments establish those conclusions. A credible review separates what was done, how it was used, the observed effect and what remains uncertain.

Activity describes the work delivered, such as a revised notice or an explanation provided. Use concerns whether the new arrangement actually appeared in the process. Effect concerns what happened for the task, such as whether a reader could identify the next step or whether an appropriately defined completion measure changed. These are related but different. A high activity total cannot automatically stand in for a better result, and one useful result should not be dismissed merely because it does not answer every structural question.

Keep comparison accurate. A later period may differ in participants, timing, definitions, assistance or wider conditions. If an authorized measure changes, examine whether the comparison is meaningful before attributing the difference solely to the notice. Describe what supports the proposed connection and what remains unknown. A practice simulation can help a team compare possibilities, but a simulated result is not an observed field outcome or a validated prediction of a person’s future result.

Ask whether the change reached the relevant mechanism. Readers may find the notice clearer while a contact barrier remains. A revised contact arrangement may help some people while another document step continues to create burden. The structural map should remain useful after the first action, showing which connection changed and which needs attention. Do not close the inquiry merely because the team delivered its planned activity. Use the evidence to select another proportionate question or an appropriate decision route.

Preserve missing experience. People who did not respond may not have received the invitation, may have another concern or may have chosen not to participate. The report cannot assume approval, disinterest or success from silence. A missing category or an incomplete record also needs an honest limit. Use approved methods and responsible data guidance for a further inquiry. Do not infer race from names, collect unnecessary personal histories or invent a numerical disclosure rule to make the analysis look complete.

Accountability should name work and responsibility. Which role authorized the change, which team will examine its use and which decision comes next? Staff should retain their equity inquiry and develop capacity, using consultant guidance, knowledge and feedback when helpful. The consultant’s program leadership does not mean doing every analysis for every team or acting as a universal permission gate. A clear handoff identifies the actual decision and evidence without making responsibility disappear between people.

Formal duties continue alongside the review. Actual records, access, eligibility, legal and employment matters use their responsible processes. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors must immediately report applicable protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency affirmative-action officer. An optional learning review, participant discussion or consultant feedback does not delay that duty. A structural report also does not decide the outcome of a real protected-class complaint or replace the required agency equity-analysis procedure.

Finish with a supported statement. The practice team might say that the notice sequence was revised through its process, several readers could identify the next step more easily and the contact mechanism and later completion evidence still need examination. That account values the change without claiming all racial inequities are gone or assigning cultural stages to staff. Structural learning continues through evidence, reflection, responsible options and follow-through. The measure of progress is a more credible inquiry and meaningful authorized change over time, with the remaining work honestly visible.

inThisLesson: Preserve missing experience and formal duties.
lessons.keyStatement: A review should support the next responsible decision rather than turn activity or silence into proof of universal success.

items.title: Recognize the work actually done
items.body: The team revised a notice and explained it to colleagues. Those activities should be documented accurately. Ask whether the revision was used and how the actual task changed before calling delivery the final result. A clearer next-step account can be meaningful even while broader evidence is incomplete. The report should make the difference between activity, use and effect understandable rather than bury it in a reassuring success label.

items.title: Keep the mechanism and limit visible
items.body: A notice revision can address a sequence problem while leaving the contact arrangement or outside document step unchanged. Return to the map and evidence instead of claiming the whole structural issue is resolved. If a later measure improves, examine definitions, period and other influences. A bounded conclusion can support another action and recognize progress without presenting correlation as complete causal proof or a simulation as observed reality.

items.title: Preserve responsibility across routes
items.body: A review can name the team’s next inquiry, the role with authority and any concern that belongs with another responsible process. Staff retain their work with consultant guidance when useful. Managers and supervisors keep immediate reporting duties under MMB Policy 1436 where applicable, and actual agency analysis requirements remain active. A course does not suspend these responsibilities, decide a real complaint or attach an inferred cultural stage to a person.

tabs.label: Activity becomes universal success
tabs.body: The leader reports that all racial inequities are eliminated because a notice and training were delivered. The activities may be important, but they do not establish every mechanism or effect. Ask whether the change was used, what the relevant evidence shows and whose experience is missing. A credible account can value progress while leaving a serious remaining question open rather than treating uncertainty as a threat to the team’s accomplishment.

tabs.label: The useful change is dismissed
tabs.body: The leader says the revision means nothing because the team did not solve every wider condition. This can overlook a real improvement and discourage responsible action within authority. Describe the bounded result and its limitation, then connect it with the next structural question. A meaningful sequence revision and an unresolved contact barrier can both be true. Accountability requires understanding that relationship, not choosing between total success and total failure.

tabs.label: Evidence and responsibility continue
tabs.body: The leader separates delivery, use and effect, checks comparison limits, identifies missing experience and names an authorized next inquiry. Formal duties remain active and staff retain the analysis with useful guidance. This account supports continued improvement without a personal cultural score, unsupported causal claim or invented legal exception. It gives the next decision a usable foundation and keeps the agency’s responsibility visible across roles and over time.

check.question: A revised notice and some positive comments are available, but broader evidence remains incomplete. What should the report say?
check.correct: Describe the actual revision and observed feedback, preserve their scope and missing evidence, and identify a responsible next inquiry.
wrong: All racial inequities have been eliminated permanently.
Every colleague has reached the same assessed IDI orientation.
Nonrespondents approved the change, so the remaining gap can be closed.
check.feedbackCorrect: This makes real progress visible and keeps the evidence and responsibility needed for further work intact.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A revision and bounded feedback do not establish permanent elimination of racial inequity. They are not a cultural assessment of colleagues. Nonresponse cannot prove approval or explain the missing experience. Separate activity, use and effect, examine comparison limits and identify the next responsible question while formal duties continue.

items.text: The approved notice revision is now used in the process.
Does a comparable later completion measure support a change in the relevant gap?
Every person has the same assessed cultural orientation after training.
Several readers found the next step easier to identify.
What did people who missed the invitation experience?
Missing feedback proves all racial barriers have disappeared.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to connect a racial pattern, a mechanism, an authorized option and honest review.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Leader Paul has a revised notice, staff activity counts and some useful reader feedback. Contact access and comparable completion evidence remain unresolved. Paul wants to declare all racial barriers eliminated and ask the consultant to own every remaining task. An actual protected-class concern must also continue through its formal route.
scenario.prompt: Which account and follow-through should Paul choose?
options: Claim complete success and close every remaining question because training was delivered.
Describe the change and bounded evidence, name the next responsible inquiry, preserve staff ownership and keep formal duties active.
Treat missing feedback as approval and assign every colleague an IDI label.
responses: Delivery is not proof of every effect. The response hides an unresolved mechanism and missing evidence.
This recognizes meaningful progress while preserving the limits and responsibility needed for continued structural work.
Silence is not approval, and the review is not a personal assessment. Neither inference supports the next decision.

lessons.transfer: Draft a review paragraph for one practice or authorized improvement. Include the actual change, evidence, limit, next responsible role and any formal route that remains active.

move.control: You can make progress and uncertainty understandable and give the next decision a supported foundation.
move.failure: The review treats activity, simulation or silence as universal proof, assigns personal labels or lets responsibility vanish between roles.
move.next: Confirm one next review question and authorized role, then write a conclusion whose strength matches the evidence.

jobAid.subtitle: Move from a racial-equity concern to a supported mechanism, option and review.
remember: Intent, observed effect and supported cause are different questions.
Keep race and connected systems visible without profiling individuals.
Staff retain their analysis; actual formal processes and duties remain active.

sections.heading: Build the inquiry
items: State the actual concern and decision within scope.
Map individual actions, institutional practices and wider connections.
Confirm current requirements, data authority, definitions and source limits.
Hear relevant affected experience through an honest participation role.

sections.heading: Act and review
items: Compare options against the mechanism, evidence, constraints and responsible authority.
Use the applicable agency equity-analysis and formal decision processes for actual qualifying work.
Describe delivery, use, effect and uncertainty separately.
Name the next responsible inquiry, preserve privacy and keep formal reporting duties active.
